name: Mughal Empire

areaKm2.note: Seshat codes 3.2-4.5 million km2 for 1700. The world_1650 polygon measures ~2.73 million km2 and predates the 1686-87 annexation of Bijapur and Golconda, so it understates 1690.

population.note: Seshat codes 110-150 million for 1700. High extended to 160M: OWID/HYDE gives India 165M, Pakistan 13.6M and Bangladesh 15.4M for 1700 (whole subcontinent ~194M, https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true); the Mughals did not rule the far south, Assam or the Maratha hill country.

urbanization.note: Habib and Moosvi put the urban share at ~15% (1600-1700, 23M urban by 1700); Tim Dyson considers this exaggerated and puts it under 9%. Mid splits the two.

activePersonnel.note: Lahori (1647) lists 200,000 stipendiary cavalry, 185,000 other cavalry and 40,000 garrisoned musketeers and gunners (~425,000); Rosen uses 550,000 for the Mughal military; Aurangzeb took ~170,000 cavalry to the Deccan (Eraly 2007 p. 300). All via the article. Counted: mansabdari contingents (paid via jagirs, standing), ahadis, walashahi guards, imperial infantry and gunners, fleet crews.

trainedReserves.note: Zamindari retainers and local militia: the Ain-i-Akbari census gives ~4.4 million (Barua 2005 p. 47, Rosen considers it pragmatic); Kolff reads it as an inventory of military labour available for hire rather than an army. Raychaudhuri/Eraly 26 million raw pool rejected. Counted as levy per the convention.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Artillery corps under the Mir-i-Atish, elephant drivers, Bengal fleet crews (Dhaka fleet: 768 boats with 933 Portuguese crew and 8,112 artillery personnel, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_of_the_Mughal_Empire), engineers and staff.

mobilizationRatio.note: Barua (2005 p. 47): the Ain-i-Akbari 4 million soldiers equalled ~3% of the Indian population in 1600.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Lahori 1647: 200,000 stipendiary (mansabdari) cavalry; Mughal heavy horse in mail, lamellar or half-plate on Turki and Arab horses (Gommans 2002 p. 114-120 via the article).

quality.note: Rubric 0.75: mail-and-plate, composite bow, lance, two horses per trooper; among the best cavalry of the era.

training.note: Rubric 0.75: professional troopers of the mansabdars.

count.note: Lahori 1647: 185,000 other cavalry (princes, faujdars, Rajput and Afghan contingents); scaled down for those on campaign or at garrisons. Range up to the 1647 figure.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5: era-typical horse archers and lancers, lower-grade horses (tattus).

count.note: Lahori 1647: 40,000 garrisoned musketeers and gunners (low); plus banduqchi matchlockmen raised by mansabdars (educated scaling).

quality.note: Rubric 0.5 minus: matchlocks; Mughals paid insufficient attention to firearm quality (Roy, via the article).

training.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: ill-paid, ill-equipped, lacking discipline (article on the ahsam infantry).

count.note: Educated guess. Shamsherbaz swordsmen, Mridha archers, sebandi revenue infantry with field forces.

Akbar kept 5,000-7,000 in the fil-khana; Moosvi estimates 5,000, Sukumar 12,000-40,000 under Jahangir (all via the article). Count = war-capable elephants with field armies; most were baggage animals.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: armoured (bargustawan-i-pil), some carrying swivel guns (gajnal).

count.note: Educated guess. Heavy siege guns, bronze light field guns, zamburak camel guns and rockets under the Mir-i-Atish; Bernier saw Aurangzeb take 200-300 camel guns to Kashmir (via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_of_the_Mughal_Empire). Field and siege pieces, swivel guns excluded.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5: heavy guns hard to move, some burst; light bronze pieces useful.

training.note: Rubric 0.5: specialised corps, many European gunners.

count.note: Bengal river fleet (nawara): the Dhaka fleet held 768 vessels (UNESCO via the article); ghurabs of 14 guns and 50-60 crew. Mid allows for the Indus and Gujarat flotillas being small.

quality.note: Rubric 0.5: river craft, effective against Ahom and Arakanese.

training.note: Rubric 0.5 minus: officers often hired Europeans.

count.note: Educated guess. Seagoing warships of the Siddi admirals of Janjira (Mughal naval arm on the west coast) that blockaded Bombay in 1689 (via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_of_the_Mughal_Empire).

quality.note: Rubric 0.5 minus: outclassed by English and Portuguese ships.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5-0.75: Aurangzeb and his generals took Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687) and captured Sambhaji (1689), but could not end Maratha guerrilla war.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: mansabdar contingents loyal to their commanders; jagir shortage after the Deccan conquests strained loyalty.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5: recent victories offset by a decade of attritional campaigning in the Deccan.

weapons.note: Anchor 5 (1600): matchlocks, heavy bronze and iron guns, mortars, rockets; no flintlocks or bayonets yet.

ships.note: Anchor 4-5: river ghurabs and armed merchantmen up to 1,600 t (Ganj-i-Sawai, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_of_the_Mughal_Empire).

fortification.note: Anchor 4-5: massive masonry forts (Agra, Lahore, Daulatabad, Golconda) without bastioned trace.

logistics.note: Anchor 5 minus: banjara grain convoys, camp markets financed by hundi credit (Gommans 2002 p. 105 via the article), river transport.

communications.note: Anchor 5: dak chowki relay posts and imperial newswriters.

isr.note: Anchor 4-5: waqia-navis newswriters and harkara spies.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Most of the jama (Aurangzeb ~450 million rupees a year, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurangzeb) was assigned to mansabdars to maintain troops; low = peacetime, mid = Deccan war.

industrialShare.note: Moosvi: late-16th-century secondary sector 18% of the economy (via the article).

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. High land revenue (a third or more of the crop) fed large towns and armies.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the other pre-modern snapshots.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Grand Trunk road (Kabul-Lahore-Agra-Bengal) and the Agra-Burhanpur-Deccan and Agra-Ajmer-Ahmedabad highways with sarais.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Surat, Hugli, Dhaka, Chittagong, Masulipatnam, Thatta, Cambay, Balasore.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Indian-owned ocean shipping at Surat and Bengal; the Ganj-i-Sawai alone was ~1,600 t (via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_of_the_Mughal_Empire).

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Moving camp-cities supplied by banjara bullock trains and local markets; the court campaigned in the Deccan for 25 years.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Bullocks of the banjara carriers, camels, horses and elephants.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.1-1.2: fortified cities and local supply; zamindar and Maratha hostility in the Deccan reduces population support.

notes: Snapshot = 1690, Aurangzeb at the empire's greatest extent after the conquest of Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687) and the capture of Sambhaji (1689), with the court in the Deccan. Personnel convention: mansabdari cavalry, ahadis, imperial infantry and gunners are activePersonnel (paid standing forces); zamindari militia and retainers (the Ain-i-Akbari 4.4 million) are trainedReserves. Mughal army sizes come from Persian court records (Ain-i-Akbari, Lahori) as read by Roy, Barua, Rosen, Kolff and Gommans via the Army of the Mughal Empire article; Gommans (Mughal Warfare, 2002) not consulted directly. Population convention: the area under direct Mughal administration in 1690; the unconquered far south, Assam and Maratha-held hill country excluded. The world_1650 polygon is the nearest file containing the empire and misses the 1686-87 Deccan annexations.
